questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an access modifier in Java?
questions.title: NOT a Java access modifier
options: private
protected
friend
public
questions.answer: friend

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Java has exactly 4 access levels: `private`, `default` (package-private, no keyword), `protected`, `public`.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Keywords like **`friend`** (a C++ concept) or **`internal`** (a C# concept) are NOT Java access modifiers — Java has no `friend` or `internal` keyword.

questions.question: Which concept allows one interface to work across multiple data types?
questions.title: One interface working across multiple data types
options: Polymorphism
Encapsulation
Inheritance
Data hiding
questions.answer: Polymorphism

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Polymorphism** (specifically generics/parametric polymorphism, or interface-based polymorphism) allows one interface/method signature to operate uniformly across multiple data types.

questions.question: What is the difference between composition and aggregation?
questions.title: Composition vs Aggregation
options: In composition the part cannot outlive the whole; in aggregation it can
In composition the part can outlive the whole; in aggregation it cannot
They are identical terms for inheritance
Composition is an is-a relationship; aggregation is has-a
questions.answer: In composition the part cannot outlive the whole; in aggregation it can

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Both are "has-a" relationships (UML associations), differing in ownership/lifecycle dependency.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: In **Composition**, the child object cannot exist independently of the parent — if the parent is destroyed, so is the child (strong "owns-a" relationship, e.g., House and Room). In **Aggregation**, the child can exist independently of the parent (weak "has-a" relationship, e.g., Department and Professor — the professor exists even if the department is dissolved).

questions.question: What is the result of calling a static method via an object reference?
questions.title: Calling a static method via an object reference
options: Compile-time error
It compiles and runs; the call is resolved by the reference's declared type
The overridden version is chosen at runtime
Runtime error because static methods need an object
questions.answer: It compiles and runs; the call is resolved by the reference's declared type

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: It **compiles and runs successfully** — Java resolves it at compile time based on the reference's declared type, but this is discouraged style since static methods belong to the class, not the instance (no polymorphic/dynamic behavior occurs).

questions.question: What does the 'extends' keyword signify in Java?
questions.title: 'extends' keyword
options: Creation of an object
Implementation of an interface
Inheritance from a parent class
Declaring a package
questions.answer: Inheritance from a parent class

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: `extends` signifies **inheritance** — a class extending another class inherits its fields and methods (or an interface extending another interface inherits its abstract methods).

questions.question: Which design pattern provides a unified high-level interface to a set of complex interfaces in a subsystem, thereby making the subsystem significantly easier to use?
questions.title: Design pattern — unified high-level interface to subsystem
options: Singleton
Observer
Adapter
Facade
questions.answer: Facade

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **Facade design pattern** — it provides a simplified, unified interface to a complex set of subsystem classes.

questions.question: In object-oriented programming, the "Diamond Problem" represents a critical structural ambiguity that arises exclusively under which specific inheritance condition?
questions.title: Diamond Problem — condition
options: Single inheritance
Multiple inheritance
Multilevel inheritance
Method overloading
questions.answer: Multiple inheritance

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The Diamond Problem arises exclusively under **multiple inheritance**, specifically when a class inherits from two classes that both inherit from a common base class, creating ambiguity about which inherited version of a member to use.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the finalize() method in Java?
questions.title: Purpose of finalize()
options: Allocate memory for a new object
Perform cleanup just before the object is garbage collected
Close the JVM
Force immediate garbage collection
questions.answer: Perform cleanup just before the object is garbage collected

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: `finalize()` was intended to let an object **perform cleanup actions (like releasing resources) just before it is garbage collected**. It's deprecated/unreliable in modern Java since GC timing isn't guaranteed — try-with-resources/AutoCloseable is preferred now.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes method hiding in Java?
questions.title: Method hiding in Java
options: A method is declared private and final
Two methods share a name but differ in parameters
A subclass defines a static method with the same signature as a static method in its superclass
A subclass overrides an instance method of its superclass
questions.answer: A subclass defines a static method with the same signature as a static method in its superclass

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Method hiding occurs when a **subclass defines a static method with the same signature as a static method in the superclass** — the subclass's version "hides" (rather than overrides) the parent version, and which one runs is decided at compile time based on the reference type, not the runtime object.

questions.question: Under the architectural guidelines of Dependency Injection, how should high-level operational modules interact with low-level data access modules?
questions.title: Dependency Injection — high-level vs low-level modules
options: High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete low-level classes
Both modules should share global variables
Low-level modules should depend on high-level classes
High-level modules should instantiate low-level classes directly
questions.answer: High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete low-level classes

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Under DI (following the Dependency Inversion Principle), **high-level modules should depend on abstractions (interfaces), not on concrete low-level implementations** — the actual low-level module instance is "injected" from outside, so high-level code never directly instantiates or depends on low-level details.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a class and an object?
questions.title: Class vs Object
options: A class is a runtime instance; an object is a blueprint
They are the same thing
A class stores only methods; an object stores only fields
A class is a blueprint; an object is a runtime instance of it
questions.answer: A class is a blueprint; an object is a runtime instance of it

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **class is a blueprint/template** defining structure (fields) and behavior (methods), while an **object is a runtime instance** of that class occupying actual memory with concrete field values.

questions.question: What specific vulnerability is completely prevented by utilizing 'immutable objects' within highly concurrent multi-threaded application architectures?
questions.title: Immutable objects — vulnerability prevented
options: Race conditions from concurrent modification
Stack overflow
Memory leaks
Deadlock due to lock ordering
questions.answer: Race conditions from concurrent modification

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Immutable objects completely prevent **race conditions/data corruption from concurrent modification (thread-safety issues)** — since their state can never change after construction, multiple threads can safely read them without synchronization.

questions.question: Which of these cannot be overridden in Java?
questions.title: Cannot be overridden in Java
options: final methods
abstract methods
Protected methods
Public instance methods
questions.answer: final methods

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **`static` methods, `final` methods, and `private` methods** cannot be overridden (static can be hidden, final is explicitly locked, private isn't inherited/visible to subclasses).

questions.question: What does the term "object slicing" refer to in C++?
questions.title: Object slicing (C++)
options: Casting a pointer to void*
Assigning a derived object to a base object by value, losing the derived part
Splitting a class into two files
Deleting an object through a base pointer
questions.answer: Assigning a derived object to a base object by value, losing the derived part

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Object slicing occurs when a **derived class object is assigned to a base class object (by value, not by pointer/reference)** — the derived-specific members are "sliced off," leaving only the base part, losing polymorphic behavior.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly illustrates the Liskov Substitution Principle?
questions.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) illustration
options: Classes are open for extension but closed for modification
A subclass object can replace its superclass object without breaking program correctness
A class should have only one reason to change
Clients should not depend on interfaces they do not use
questions.answer: A subclass object can replace its superclass object without breaking program correctness

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: LSP is illustrated when **a subclass object can be substituted for its superclass object anywhere in the program without altering the correctness/behavior of that program** — e.g., a `Square` violates LSP if substituting it for `Rectangle` breaks expected behavior (like independent width/height setting).

questions.question: What is the effect of making a constructor private in a class?
questions.title: Private constructor effect
options: The class becomes abstract automatically
The class cannot be inherited by any class
Objects can be created only inside static blocks of other classes
The class cannot be instantiated from outside the class
questions.answer: The class cannot be instantiated from outside the class

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A private constructor **prevents the class from being instantiated directly from outside the class** — commonly used for Singleton patterns, utility classes with only static members, or factory-method-controlled instantiation.

questions.question: What is constructor injection in Dependency Injection?
questions.title: Constructor injection
options: The class creates its own dependencies with new
Dependencies are looked up from a global registry
Dependencies are supplied to a class through its constructor
Dependencies are set through setter methods after creation
questions.answer: Dependencies are supplied to a class through its constructor

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Constructor injection is a form of Dependency Injection where **dependencies are provided to a class through its constructor parameters at the time of object creation**, ensuring the object is always created in a fully valid, dependency-satisfied state.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about Java interfaces after Java 9?
questions.title: Java interfaces after Java 9
options: Interfaces can have instance fields
Interfaces can have constructors
Interfaces can extend multiple classes
Interfaces can have private methods
questions.answer: Interfaces can have private methods

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Since Java 9, interfaces can also have **private methods** (in addition to the `default` and `static` methods introduced in Java 8) — private methods let default/static methods share common code without exposing it publicly.

questions.question: What executes when a child class object is referenced by a parent type and an overridden method is called?
questions.title: Child object referenced by parent type, overridden method called
options: The method of the reference's declared type
A compile-time error
The overridden method in the child class
The parent class version of the method
questions.answer: The overridden method in the child class

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **child class's (overridden) version of the method executes** — this is runtime/dynamic polymorphism, resolved based on the actual object type, not the reference type.

questions.question: What is the significance of the transient keyword in Java?
questions.title: `transient` keyword significance
options: The field is stored in the stack
The field cannot be modified after initialization
The field is excluded from default serialization
The field is shared across threads
questions.answer: The field is excluded from default serialization

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: `transient` marks a field to be **excluded from the default Java serialization process** — its value won't be saved when the object is serialized, and it will be reset to its default value upon deserialization.

questions.question: Which of the following Object-Oriented design principles explicitly states that subclasses should be replaceable for their base classes without altering the correctness of the program?
questions.title: Principle: subclasses replaceable for base classes
options: Open/Closed Principle
Liskov Substitution Principle
Single Responsibility Principle
Interface Segregation Principle
questions.answer: Liskov Substitution Principle

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This is the **Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)**, one of the SOLID principles.

questions.question: What is the main use of the hashCode() method in Java?
questions.title: hashCode() main use
options: Returns the object's memory size
Creates a copy of the object
Compares two objects for equality
Provides an integer used to place objects in hash-based collections
questions.answer: Provides an integer used to place objects in hash-based collections

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: `hashCode()` returns an integer used to **determine the bucket/index at which an object is stored in hash-based collections** (like `HashMap`, `HashSet`), enabling fast lookup; it must be consistent with `equals()` (equal objects must have equal hash codes).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the Dependency Inversion Principle?
questions.title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
options: Abstractions should depend on implementation details
High-level and low-level modules should both depend on abstractions
Every class should have exactly one interface
High-level modules should depend directly on low-level modules
questions.answer: High-level and low-level modules should both depend on abstractions

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: DIP states that **high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules — both should depend on abstractions; and abstractions should not depend on details — details should depend on abstractions.**

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT allowed in Java?
questions.title: NOT allowed in Java
options: Method overloading
Multiple inheritance of classes
Static nested classes
Implementing multiple interfaces
questions.answer: Multiple inheritance of classes

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Java does **not allow multiple inheritance of classes** (a class extending more than one class), operator overloading, or pointer arithmetic — these are common "not allowed" answers depending on exact options; multiple class inheritance is the classic one.

questions.question: What is covariant return type in Java method overriding?
questions.title: Covariant return type
options: An overriding method must return exactly the same type
An overriding method may return a subtype of the overridden method's return type
An overriding method may return any unrelated type
An overriding method must return void
questions.answer: An overriding method may return a subtype of the overridden method's return type

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A covariant return type allows an **overriding method in a subclass to return a more specific (narrower/subtype) return type than the method it overrides in the superclass**, instead of requiring the exact same return type.

questions.question: In Java, when a class implements multiple interfaces that contain conflicting default methods with the exact same signature, how is the ambiguity definitively resolved?
questions.title: Conflicting default methods from multiple interfaces
options: The first interface listed wins automatically
The method from the last interface wins
The conflicting methods are merged automatically
The class must explicitly override the method to resolve the conflict
questions.answer: The class must explicitly override the method to resolve the conflict

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Java forces the implementing class to **explicitly override the method and resolve the conflict itself** (often calling a specific interface's version via `InterfaceName.super.methodName()`) — it will not compile otherwise.

questions.question: In Java, what is the difference between == and equals() when comparing objects?
questions.title: == vs equals()
options: == compares content; equals() compares references
Both always compare references
Both always compare content
== compares references; equals() compares logical content
questions.answer: == compares references; equals() compares logical content

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: `==` compares **reference/memory address equality** (whether two variables point to the exact same object), while `equals()` (when properly overridden) compares **logical/content equality** (whether two objects have the same meaningful value, even if they're different instances).

questions.question: What is the key difference between early binding and late binding?
questions.title: Early binding vs late binding
options: Early binding resolves at compile time; late binding resolves at runtime
Early binding resolves at runtime; late binding at compile time
Both resolve at compile time
Both resolve at runtime
questions.answer: Early binding resolves at compile time; late binding resolves at runtime

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Early (static) binding** resolves method calls **at compile time** based on the reference type (used for overloading, static/private/final methods). **Late (dynamic) binding** resolves method calls **at runtime** based on the actual object type (used for overriding/polymorphism).

questions.question: In Object-Oriented theory, which principle refers to the ability of an internal module to hide its exact data structure and implementation details from external objects?
questions.title: Principle: hiding internal data structure/implementation
options: Inheritance
Polymorphism
Overloading
Encapsulation
questions.answer: Encapsulation

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This is **Encapsulation** — bundling data and methods together while restricting direct external access to internal implementation details (typically via private fields and public getter/setter methods).

questions.question: What is the fundamental distinction between 'aggregation' and 'composition' in unified modeling language (UML) structural relationships?
questions.title: Aggregation vs Composition (UML)
options: Aggregation uses a dashed line; composition uses a solid line
Aggregation uses a filled diamond; composition uses a hollow diamond
Aggregation uses a hollow diamond; composition uses a filled diamond
Both use a hollow arrow
questions.answer: Aggregation uses a hollow diamond; composition uses a filled diamond

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Both represent "has-a" relationships shown with a diamond; **Aggregation uses a hollow (empty) diamond** and represents a weak relationship where the part can exist independently, while **Composition uses a filled (solid) diamond** and represents a strong relationship where the part's lifecycle is bound to the whole.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the Open/Closed Principle?
questions.title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
options: Subtypes must be substitutable for base types
High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules
Entities should be open for extension but closed for modification
A class should have only one reason to change
questions.answer: Entities should be open for extension but closed for modification

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: OCP states that **software entities (classes, modules, functions) should be open for extension but closed for modification** — new behavior should be added by extending existing code (e.g., via inheritance/interfaces), not by altering already-tested existing code.

questions.question: In C++, how does the compiler internally resolve dynamic dispatch for polymorphic method calls at runtime?
questions.title: C++ dynamic dispatch resolution mechanism
options: A virtual table (vtable) of function pointers
A copy of the base class code in each object
A hash table of method names
A switch statement generated at compile time
questions.answer: A virtual table (vtable) of function pointers

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The compiler resolves dynamic dispatch using a **virtual table (vtable)** — each class with virtual functions has a vtable of function pointers, and each object holds a hidden vptr pointing to its class's vtable; calls are resolved at runtime via this pointer.

questions.question: What happens when a class implements two interfaces with the same default method and does not override it?
questions.title: Class implements two interfaces with same default method, no override
options: The first interface's version runs
It runs without any error
It throws an exception at runtime
A compile-time error; the class must override the method
questions.answer: A compile-time error; the class must override the method

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This results in a **compile-time error** ("interface conflict/inherits unrelated defaults") — Java forces the class to explicitly override the method to resolve the ambiguity.

questions.question: What is a virtual function in C++?
questions.title: Virtual function (C++)
options: A function that is always inlined
A function that cannot be overridden
A function defined only in an abstract class
A base-class member function declared virtual that derived classes can override
questions.answer: A base-class member function declared virtual that derived classes can override

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A virtual function is a **member function declared in a base class using the `virtual` keyword that can be overridden in a derived class**, enabling runtime polymorphism — the correct overridden version is called based on the actual object type, even when accessed via a base class pointer/reference.

questions.question: In C#, what is the definitive functional purpose of a 'virtual' method when explicitly declared inside a parent class structure?
questions.title: C# 'virtual' method purpose
options: It makes the method private
It prevents the method from being overridden
It allows derived classes to override the method
It makes the method static
questions.answer: It allows derived classes to override the method

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Declaring a method `virtual` in a parent class **allows derived classes to override it (using the `override` keyword)**, enabling runtime polymorphism; without `virtual`, the method cannot be overridden (only hidden with `new`).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the default method in a Java interface (since Java 8)?
questions.title: Purpose of default method in Java interface (Java 8+)
options: Provide a method body in an interface without breaking existing implementers
Replace abstract classes entirely
Allow interfaces to hold instance variables
Make the interface instantiable
questions.answer: Provide a method body in an interface without breaking existing implementers

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Default methods let interfaces **provide a method implementation with a body**, allowing new methods to be added to interfaces **without breaking existing classes** that already implement that interface (they inherit the default implementation automatically).

questions.question: In Java, what is an instance initializer block used for?
questions.title: Instance initializer block
options: Run once when the class is loaded
Run only when an object is destroyed
Run code each time an object is created, before the constructor body
Run when a method is overridden
questions.answer: Run code each time an object is created, before the constructor body

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: An instance initializer block (a `{ }` block at class level, not inside a method) **runs every time an object is created, right before the constructor body executes** (after `super()` call) — used to initialize instance variables or run common setup logic shared across multiple constructors.

questions.question: What is the result of calling an unimplemented abstract method?
questions.title: Calling an unimplemented abstract method
options: It returns null
It throws NullPointerException
It cannot be called directly; a concrete subclass must implement it first
It runs an empty default body
questions.answer: It cannot be called directly; a concrete subclass must implement it first

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: You **cannot call an abstract method directly on an abstract class** (and cannot instantiate an abstract class at all); it must be overridden with a concrete implementation in a subclass before it can be invoked on an actual object.

questions.question: In Java, which scenario would cause a StackOverflowError?
questions.title: Scenario causing StackOverflowError
options: Dividing an integer by zero
Allocating a very large array on the heap
Opening too many files
Infinite or very deep recursion
questions.answer: Infinite or very deep recursion

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Uncontrolled/infinite recursion** (a method that keeps calling itself without a proper base case to stop) causes a StackOverflowError, as each call adds a new frame to the call stack until it exceeds the stack's size limit.

questions.question: What type of memory holds newly instantiated objects in Java?
questions.title: Memory holding newly instantiated objects
options: Register memory
Stack
Heap
Method area only
questions.answer: Heap

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **Heap** memory holds newly instantiated objects in Java (the Stack holds method call frames and local primitive/reference variables).

questions.question: What type of inheritance is not supported by Java classes?
questions.title: Inheritance type not supported by Java classes
options: Single inheritance
Multiple inheritance of classes
Hierarchical inheritance
Multilevel inheritance
questions.answer: Multiple inheritance of classes

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Java classes do **not support multiple inheritance** (a class extending more than one class) — this is avoided to prevent the Diamond Problem; Java allows multiple inheritance only through interfaces.

questions.question: What is the definitive operational consequence of declaring a class constructor as 'explicit' in C++?
questions.title: C++ 'explicit' constructor
options: It makes the constructor run automatically
It makes the constructor private
It prevents implicit conversions through that constructor
It prevents the class from being inherited
questions.answer: It prevents implicit conversions through that constructor

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Declaring a constructor `explicit` **prevents the compiler from using it for implicit type conversions** (implicit single-argument conversions) — the constructor can then only be called explicitly, avoiding accidental/unintended object creation via implicit conversion.

questions.question: Which creational design pattern is strictly engineered to guarantee that a specific class possesses exactly one instance while providing a global access point to it?
questions.title: Creational pattern guaranteeing exactly one instance
options: Observer
Builder
Singleton
Factory
questions.answer: Singleton

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **Singleton design pattern** ensures a class has exactly one instance and provides a single global access point to it.

questions.question: What is dynamic dispatch in OOP?
questions.title: Dynamic dispatch (OOP)
options: The method to call is chosen at runtime from the object's actual type
The method is chosen at compile time from the reference type
The method is chosen by the linker
The method is chosen by the number of arguments
questions.answer: The method to call is chosen at runtime from the object's actual type

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Dynamic dispatch is the mechanism by which **the specific implementation of an overridden method to invoke is determined at runtime based on the actual (runtime) type of the object**, rather than the type of the reference variable — the core mechanism enabling runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: What specific memory management issue occurs in C++ if a base class pointer deletes a derived class object, but the base class does not possess a virtual destructor?
questions.title: Base pointer deletes derived object, no virtual destructor (C++)
options: The program fails to compile
The derived destructor runs correctly
Undefined behavior — typically the derived part is not destroyed, leaking resources
The base object is copied
questions.answer: Undefined behavior — typically the derived part is not destroyed, leaking resources

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This causes **undefined behavior, typically a memory leak** — only the base class's destructor runs (not the derived class's), so any resources allocated specifically by the derived class are never released.

questions.question: Which statement is true about a static nested class in Java?
questions.title: Static nested class in Java
options: It cannot have static members
It can access outer instance fields directly
It can be instantiated without an instance of the outer class
It needs an outer instance to be created
questions.answer: It can be instantiated without an instance of the outer class

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A static nested class **does not require an instance of the outer class to be created** — it behaves like a top-level class placed inside another class for namespacing, and it cannot directly access the outer class's non-static (instance) members without an explicit outer object reference.

questions.question: Which design principle does a class that handles both database access and user login violate?
questions.title: Class handling both DB access and user login — violated principle
options: Liskov Substitution Principle
Open/Closed Principle
Single Responsibility Principle
Dependency Inversion Principle
questions.answer: Single Responsibility Principle

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This violates the **Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)** — a class should have only one reason to change, but this class has two unrelated responsibilities (data persistence and authentication logic).

questions.question: In the context of the SOLID principles, what is the primary objective of the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)?
questions.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) objective
options: Subclasses must be replaceable for base classes
Modules should depend on abstractions
A class should have one reason to change
Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use
questions.answer: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: ISP states that **clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces/methods they do not use** — large, general-purpose interfaces should be split into smaller, more specific ones so implementing classes only need to know about the methods relevant to them.

questions.question: In Java, what is the exact operational effect of applying the 'final' keyword to an explicitly defined object reference variable?
questions.title: `final` keyword on an object reference variable
options: The object cannot be garbage collected
The object becomes immutable
The reference cannot be reassigned, but the object's state can still change
The reference becomes null
questions.answer: The reference cannot be reassigned, but the object's state can still change

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Making a reference variable `final` means **the reference itself cannot be reassigned to point to a different object after initialization** — however, the object's internal state can still be mutated (if the object itself isn't immutable); only the reference binding is fixed.

questions.question: Which access modifier allows access only within the same package?
questions.title: Access modifier — access only within same package
options: protected
Default (package-private)
public
private
questions.answer: Default (package-private)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **default (no modifier / package-private)** access level restricts access to classes within the same package only — it's more restrictive than `protected` (which also allows subclasses in other packages) and less restrictive than `private`.

questions.question: What problem does the Observer design pattern solve?
questions.title: What problem does the Observer design pattern solve?
options: Notifying multiple dependent objects automatically when one object's state changes
Ensuring only one instance of a class exists
Providing a simplified interface to a complex subsystem
Allowing incompatible interfaces to work together
questions.answer: Notifying multiple dependent objects automatically when one object's state changes

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Observer is a behavioral design pattern establishing a one-to-many dependency between objects.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **The Observer pattern lets one 'subject' object automatically notify a list of registered 'observer' objects whenever its state changes**, without the subject needing to know the concrete details of its observers — commonly used in event-handling systems and UI frameworks.

questions.question: What is method overloading, and how is it resolved by the compiler?
questions.title: What is method overloading, and how is it resolved by the co
options: Multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists, resolved at compile time
A subclass replacing a parent method's behavior, resolved at runtime
Two classes sharing a common interface
A method that can only be called once per object
questions.answer: Multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists, resolved at compile time

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Overloading is a form of compile-time (static) polymorphism, distinct from overriding (runtime polymorphism).

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Method overloading means defining multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists (number, type, or order of parameters)** — the compiler decides which version to call based on the arguments passed at the call site (compile-time/static binding).

questions.question: Why does the 'diamond problem' NOT occur with Java interfaces the same way it does with C++ multiple class inheritance?
questions.title: Why does the 'diamond problem' NOT occur with Java interface
options: Java requires explicit resolution of conflicting default methods instead of silently picking one
Java interfaces cannot have any methods at all
Java doesn't allow a class to implement more than one interface
Interfaces in Java automatically rename conflicting methods
questions.answer: Java requires explicit resolution of conflicting default methods instead of silently picking one

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Since Java 8, interfaces can have default methods with bodies, reintroducing a diamond-like risk when a class implements two interfaces with the same default method.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Java sidesteps ambiguity by forcing the implementing class to explicitly override the conflicting method (optionally calling a specific interface's version via `InterfaceName.super.method()`)** — the compiler flags an error instead of silently choosing one implementation, unlike C++'s implicit multiple inheritance ambiguity.
